# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is lazy. Left alone, it sits still, and if you want it to move—to flow through pipes, up into buildings, out of a faucet on the fortieth floor—you have to give it a reason. The entire engineering discipline of municipal water supply is, at its heart, the management of one simple physical fact: water only flows where pressure tells it to. Understanding how a modern city moves water from a reservoir to the top of a skyscraper means understanding where that pressure comes from, how it's measured, and how engineers keep it steady even as demand surges, pumps fail, and pipes get repaired.

## The Fundamental Currency: Head

Engineers describe water pressure in terms of "head," which is simply the height of a column of water. If you have a tank of water sitting 100 feet above a faucet, the water at that faucet experiences pressure equivalent to that 100-foot column—about 43 pounds per square inch (psi). This is why elevation is the cheapest pump ever invented. A reservoir placed on a hill above a city provides pressure for free, courtesy of gravity, and many older cities were designed around exactly this arrangement.
